cuts.question_text: What is a conjugate acid-base pair?

s4_hco3.label: Closing line — the definition boxed

lines.text: Conjugate pair = an acid and a base that differ by exactly one H⁺

s4_hco3.why: The boxed line repeats the one-proton difference so the examiner sees the point of the definition at a glance. This 2-mark form carries no HCO₃⁻ working at all — HCO₃⁻ belongs to the 4-mark form, where this same step holds part (b). page_header: Chemical Equilibrium, Acids and Bases · 4 marks

steps.label: The definition
lines: An acid and a base that differ by exactly
one proton (H⁺) form a conjugate acid-base
The conjugate acid has one proton more;
the conjugate base has one proton less.
steps.why: The whole idea is the one-proton difference: every Brønsted-Lowry acid turns into its conjugate base by giving one H⁺, and every base turns into its conjugate acid by taking one.
common_mistakes: Writing that the pair differs by one electron. The difference is one proton, H⁺.
Swapping the two: the species WITH the extra proton is the conjugate acid.
steps.memory_tip: More H⁺ = acid, less H⁺ = base. The pair sits one proton apart.
steps.margin_note: The words exactly one proton must appear.

steps.label: The example
lines: H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid of the base H₂O.
Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of the acid HCl.
steps.why: One equation shows both pairs at once: HCl/Cl⁻ differ by one proton, and H₂O/H₃O⁺ differ by one proton — naming which member is which proves the definition is understood.
common_mistakes: Pairing HCl with H₃O⁺. The pairs are HCl/Cl⁻ and H₂O/H₃O⁺ — each pair differs by one H⁺.
Writing the ionisation with a one-way arrow instead of ⇌.
steps.memory_tip: Every proton-transfer equation holds two pairs. Match each species with its one-proton partner.
steps.margin_note: Name which member is the conjugate acid and which the conjugate base.

steps.label: (a) OH⁻
lines: Add one H⁺ for the conjugate acid; remove
one H⁺ for the conjugate base.
steps.why: The recipe is mechanical: OH⁻ plus one H⁺ is H₂O, and OH⁻ minus one H⁺ is O²⁻. Charges change by one unit each way because a proton carries +1.
common_mistakes: Writing the conjugate base of OH⁻ as O⁻. Removing H⁺ from OH⁻ leaves O²⁻ — the charge drops by one full unit.
Giving only the conjugate acid. The question asks for both.
steps.memory_tip: Add H⁺: charge goes up by one. Remove H⁺: charge goes down by one.
steps.margin_note: Check each answer by counting H atoms and total charge.

steps.label: (b) HCO₃⁻

lines.text: OH⁻: acid H₂O, base O²⁻ · HCO₃⁻: acid H₂CO₃, base CO₃²⁻

steps.why: HCO₃⁻ can both take a proton (giving H₂CO₃) and give one (leaving CO₃²⁻), which is why it appears in this question — it shows one species can have both a conjugate acid and a conjugate base. The usual slip is writing CO₃⁻: removing one H⁺ drops the charge by a full unit, from −1 to −2, so the conjugate base is CO₃²⁻.
common_mistakes: Changing the charge by the wrong amount. Adding one H⁺ raises the charge by exactly one unit and removing one H⁺ lowers it by exactly one unit.
Forgetting that one species can have BOTH a conjugate acid and a conjugate base.
steps.memory_tip: HCO₃⁻ is the middle member of the series H₂CO₃ — HCO₃⁻ — CO₃²⁻, with one proton between neighbours.
steps.margin_note: Box the four answers together as the final summary.

insider_note: Add H⁺ for the conjugate acid, remove H⁺ for the conjugate base. Worked one species at a time, each listed species gives two one-line answers, and the charge is where marks are lost: removing H⁺ lowers the charge by one full unit. The 2-mark form asks for the definition and one example only; the 4-mark form adds the species listed in the question.
